lead: The Great Fast begins with a lesson in how to begin. Shubkono, the service of forgiveness, is its door, and the epistle (Ephesians 4:25–32) gives it words: “forgiving one another, as God in Christ has forgiven you” (4:32). Genesis gives the root: Abram, with nothing to show for God's promise, believes the God who made it. The Gospel gives the pattern: Jesus, forty days in the wilderness, answers the tempter from the word of God. Peace with one another, trust in God, and the word as our food: that is the Fast.

set: Genesis 12–25 tell the story of Abraham, who is still called Abram here. God has promised him land, descendants and blessing (12:1–3), and no child has come. “After these things” points back to chapter 14, where Abram went to war to rescue Lot. God's first word, “Do not be afraid”, suggests what is in his heart. This is the first time in Genesis that Abram's own words to God are recorded, and they are a complaint.
str: v. 1: the word of the Lord comes in a vision.
vv. 2–3: Abram's complaint: no child, and a servant as his heir.
vv. 4–5: the promise: a son of his own, and descendants like the stars.
v. 6: Abram believes, and the Lord reckons it to him as righteousness.
kw: The soldier's hand shield. God does not promise Abram a shield; he says that he himself is one. The Psalms take up the same word many times.
From the root ’āman, to be firm or solid. The word Amen comes from the same root. To believe is to rest one's whole weight on God as on firm ground.
A word for counting and crediting. Abram's trust is entered to his account as righteousness. Paul builds on this verse in Romans 4 and Galatians 3.
vv: Do not be afraid, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great.
God speaks first. The promise comes before Abram has asked for anything.
Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them.
Abram has been looking at what he lacks. God takes him outside and makes him look up. The answer to his complaint is not an explanation but a wider sky.
And he believed the Lord; and the Lord reckoned it to him as righteousness.
Nothing has changed yet: there is still no child. Abram's only act is to trust. This short verse becomes one of the most quoted in the whole New Testament teaching on faith.
ch: The Catechism presents Abraham as the model of the obedience of faith, and uses this verse in the form Paul quotes it: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (CCC 144–146). St Paul makes it the ground of his teaching in Romans 4 and Galatians 3, and St James reads it together with Abraham's obedience (James 2:21–23). At the opening of the Fast it tells us where our discipline must begin: not with what we can show God, but with what God has promised.

r.h: Forty days and the word of God
set: Matthew places this scene straight after the baptism of Jesus, where the voice from heaven says, “This is my Son, the Beloved” (3:17). The tempter now begins twice with “If you are the Son of God”. The Spirit who came down at the Jordan leads Jesus into the wilderness. Israel was tested in the wilderness for forty years (Deuteronomy 8:2). Jesus, the Son, walks that road in forty days and stays faithful. All three of his answers come from Deuteronomy.
str: vv. 1–2: led by the Spirit; the forty days of fasting.
vv. 3–4: the first test: stones into bread.
vv. 5–7: the second test: the pinnacle of the temple.
vv. 8–10: the third test: all the kingdoms of the world.
v. 11: the devil leaves, and angels wait on him.
kw: One Greek word covers both meanings. The Spirit leads Jesus to the place of testing; the devil tries to turn the testing into a fall.
Diabolos means slanderer or accuser, and Satan comes from the Hebrew word for adversary. The story uses both (4:1, 4:10).

The tense means that it stands written and still holds. Jesus uses no display of power, only the word. The devil quotes Scripture too (Psalm 91:11–12), which shows that even the word can be twisted when it is torn from its sense.
vv: He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterwards he was famished.
Moses (Exodus 34:28) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:8) also went forty days. The hunger is real: the Son is truly human, and the test comes at his weakest point.
One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.
From Deuteronomy 8:3, where Moses explains the manna. Jesus does not despise bread; he will feed crowds. He refuses to use his Sonship for himself.
Away with you, Satan! for it is written, ‘Worship the Lord your God, and serve only him.’

From Deuteronomy 6:13. The offer of all the kingdoms is a road to power without the Cross. Jesus refuses it, and at the end of the Gospel the Risen Lord says that all authority has been given to him (28:18).
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus is the new Adam, who stayed faithful where the first Adam gave in, and that he fulfils Israel's vocation perfectly (CCC 539). It adds, in the Latin Church's own wording: “By the solemn forty days of Lent the Church unites herself each year to the mystery of Jesus in the desert” (CCC 540). St John Chrysostom says that the Lord went into temptation straight after baptism so that the baptized would not be thrown into confusion when trials come (in substance, Homilies on Matthew 13). St Augustine says that in Christ we ourselves were tempted, and in him we overcome (in substance, on Psalm 60).

qa: Why does the Spirit lead Jesus to be tempted, if God tempts no one?

God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13). The Spirit leads Jesus into the place of testing, as God led Israel in the wilderness, and the evil comes from the tempter. Jesus enters our condition so that he can help us: “Because he himself was tested by what he suffered, he is able to help those who are being tested” (Hebrews 2:18).
rite: Shubkono comes from the Syriac word for forgiveness. Our Church does not start the Fast by counting foods. The priest bows before the people and asks their pardon, and the faithful ask pardon of one another. It stands beside today's epistle as its living form: “do not let the sun go down on your anger” (Ephesians 4:26). With that peace we can walk the road of the Fast together.
study: Abram believed when nothing had yet changed. Which promise of God am I finding hard to trust in this Great Fast?
Jesus answered each test from Scripture. Which word of God will I carry with me through this Fast? Whom do I need to forgive before I begin?
